intro: Every sport keeps two kinds of records. One kind lists scores and champions. The other kind lists who was allowed to enter, and who paid for the room. This unit reads the second kind. You will study entry rules that decide which bodies a league counts: nationality rules, age lines, weight classes, Paralympic sport classes and the long, contested history of the women's category.

You will also follow the government into the stadium. Public bonds built ballparks in Chicago and across the country, and companies bought the names on public walls. Eminent domain cleared land in Los Angeles and Brooklyn. Congress protected a football merger and chartered the body that runs American Olympic sport, and a 2018 court ruling let states legalize sports betting. After deadly crushes and attacks, governments also wrote rules for keeping crowds safe.

As you read, track three things for each rule: which body wrote it, in what year, and which court or law later changed it. You will be able to set two sides of a hard argument next to each other, using their own evidence, before you decide what you think.
bigQuestion: How do rule books, courts and governments decide who may play and who pays for the places where sport happens?

timeline.t: Los Angeles voters approve giving Chavez Ravine land to the Dodgers
IOC begins chromosome screening of women at the Olympic Games
Rich Stadium in Buffalo opens under an early stadium naming-rights deal
Amateur Sports Act charters the U.S. Olympic Committee
Zola Budd gains British citizenship and runs for Britain in Los Angeles
Illinois creates the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority
Hillsborough crush in Sheffield leads to the Taylor Report
Deaths of three college wrestlers lead to new NCAA weight rules
PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin requires a cart for Casey Martin
Kelo v. City of New London widens the meaning of public use
Murphy v. NCAA lets states legalize sports betting; Illinois follows in 2019

words.d: the set of rules that decides who is allowed to compete
legal membership in a country, which decides which national team an athlete may join
sorting schools or athletes into groups so that similar ones compete against each other
grouping athletes by how an impairment affects the actions of a sport
testing used by sports bodies to decide who may enter the women's category
an adjustment the law requires so an athlete with a disability can play, unless it would alter the core of the game
a public IOU that investors buy and a government repays over many years, with interest
public money or tax breaks given to help a private business or project
the government's power to take private property for public use, with payment
the purpose the Constitution requires before government can take private property
the right, sold for a fee, to put a company's name on a building or event
a legal grant from a government that creates an organization and sets its powers

test.q: How did Zola Budd become eligible to run for Britain in 1984?
choices: She gained British citizenship through her grandfather.
South Africa sent her as a guest.
test.why: Budd gained British citizenship in about two weeks through her British grandfather.

test.q: What changed in college wrestling for the 1998–99 season?
choices: The NCAA banned sweating-off methods and moved weigh-ins closer to competition.
test.why: After three wrestlers died in 1997, the NCAA rewrote its weight rules.

test.q: What did a federal judge order for Tatyana McFadden in 2006?
choices: that she race on the track at the same time as the other runners
that she join a Paralympic team
test.why: The injunction ended her separate, solo heats at her Maryland high school.

test.q: Why did the IPC suspend intellectual impairment events after 2000?
choices: The events moved to the Olympics.
A Spanish team won gold with players who had no intellectual impairment.
test.why: The Sydney 2000 basketball scandal showed the class had not been checked.

test.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin (2001)?
choices: A golf cart was a reasonable modification the ADA required.
Golf was exempt from all disability laws.
Martin was too old to compete.
The PGA Tour had to close.
test.why: The Court ruled 7–2 that the cart did not change the basic nature of the events.

test.q: Which new entry step did the IOC add for female Olympians in 1968?
choices: It opened the Games to professionals.
It began chromosome screening of female athletes.
test.why: The IOC began screening women with a cheek-cell chromosome test in 1968.

test.q: In 2021, who did the IOC say should set eligibility rules for transgender athletes?
choices: the Court of Arbitration for Sport
test.why: The IOC's 2021 framework left eligibility to international federations.

test.q: What did the 1975 Title IX sports regulation allow?
choices: only mixed teams in every sport
separate teams by sex where selection is by skill or the sport is a contact sport
test.why: The regulation allows separate teams in those cases.

test.q: Why do many economists doubt that public stadiums pay off?
choices: Studies found no case where a new stadium clearly raised local growth.
test.why: Noll and Zimbalist's 1997 studies found spending mostly shifted from other local entertainment.

test.q: What does the Fifth Amendment require before property is taken?
choices: a vote of the team owners
test.why: The Takings Clause allows takings only for public use, with just compensation.

test.q: What happened in Chavez Ravine in May 1959?
choices: Deputies removed the Aréchiga family from their home.
test.why: The last holdouts were carried from their home as cameras filmed.

test.q: Why did the Colts leave Baltimore overnight in March 1984?
choices: Maryland moved to let Baltimore seize the team by eminent domain.
test.why: The owner moved the team before the eminent domain law could take effect.

test.q: Which 2018 Supreme Court case let states legalize sports betting?
choices: Kelo v. City of New London
Federal Baseball Club v. National League
Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Association
test.why: Murphy struck down the 1992 federal law that barred most states from authorizing sports betting.

test.q: What pays back most bonds of the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority?
choices: a tax on Chicago hotel rooms
test.why: The authority's bonds are backed largely by Chicago's hotel tax.

test.q: What did the Taylor Report of 1990 call for after Hillsborough?
choices: all-seater stadiums at top English grounds
test.why: Taylor blamed failures of police crowd control and called for seats for every fan at top grounds.

write.prompt: Pick one case from this unit: an eligibility rule (Zola Budd, Sydney 2000, the women's category) or a public deal (Comiskey Park, Chavez Ravine, the 1966 merger, Illinois sports betting). Argue whether the rule or deal served the public. Cite at least two dated records from the unit, such as a court ruling, a law or a governing body's decision.
tips: Name each record exactly: the case name, the law or the body, and its year.
Say who wrote the rule or made the deal before you judge it.
Give the strongest point of the side you disagree with, in its own words.
Use the unit's terms, such as eligibility, eminent domain or public subsidy.
Keep facts and opinions apart: state what happened, then what you think.
